Les communautés marginalisées ressentent: Marginalized communities are feeling complex emotions about Charlie Kirk’s death, caught between trauma and self-protection.

Les thérapeutes affirment qu'il est norm: Therapists say it is normal for marginalized communities to feel torn, even indifferent, after the death of someone who persecuted them for years.
Pour de nombreuses personnes LGBTQ+, Cha: For many LGBTQ+ people, Charlie Kirk embodied hostility. The far-right political commentator and founder of Turning Point USA <l1>frequently disparaged LGBTQ+ people</l1>, calling trans people “<l2>real middle fingers to God</l2>,” describing homosexuality as a danger to children and <l3>labelling LGBTQ+ identities a “social contagion”</l3>.
Kirk a également fait des remarques raci: Kirk also made racial remarks, including wondering <l1>whether he would feel safe if a pilot were Black</l1> and <l2>claiming that God had cursed Black people by making them “subservient”</l2>.
Kirk étant résident de l'Arizona et fond: Because Kirk was an Arizona resident and the founder of one of the state’s most prominent conservative groups, both at the Capitol and on university campuses, his death has prompted mixed feelings, particularly within the LGBTQ+ community.
Charlie Kirk a été abattu cette semaine: Charlie Kirk was shot this week while speaking at a university event, in what appears to be a political assassination. Shortly before he was killed, he had answered an audience member’s question about mass shootings.
Les réactions à sa mort ont mis en évide: Reactions to his death have exposed deep divisions in American society. While the media and political leaders called for peace and reflection, often downplaying or glossing over Kirk’s racist and homophobic remarks, some members of the LGBTQ+ community and other groups targeted by his rhetoric showed little sadness.
« Il est normal de ne pas ressentir beau: “It’s okay not to feel much empathy for someone who built a career on refusing to show it to others,” therapist Jeff Guenther said in a post on his hugely popular Instagram account, TherapyJeff. “That doesn’t mean you’re celebrating his death. It doesn’t mean you’re heartless. It simply means your compassion has limits, and those limits are often shaped by how much compassion a person showed during their life.”
En ligne, de nombreux messages n’y vont: Online, many posts pull no punches: one meme circulating on Instagram reads: “This ultra-violent country demands that we mourn the people who wanted us dead.”
D'autres messages, provenant de personne: Other posts, from queer people, quickly pointed out that Kirk had called for Nuremberg-style trials of doctors who provide gender-affirming care, or had labelled trans people “groomers” (people who prepare children for sexual abuse) or pedophiles.
Bre Wandrych, une travailleuse sociale b: Bre Wandrych, a Phoenix-based social worker who works with LGBTQ+ clients, said her reaction reflected greater complexity: “Part of me is sad because a man died, a victim of gun violence – I don’t think anyone should die in such circumstances,” she said, explaining that she had taken the time to understand her emotions. “But part of me feels nothing for the man who championed white supremacy and bigotry. Part of me may be horrified at seeing a graphic video of a shooting, and another part may be resentful because our community doesn’t get the same level of support when it’s the victim of violence.”
Selon M<sup>me</sup> Wandrych, les conve: According to Ms.<sup></sup> Wandrych, conversations about empathy are essential to getting through moments like this one.
Les chercheurs définissent différents ty: Researchers define different types of empathy: cognitive empathy, which allows people to understand another’s point of view; emotional empathy, when people mirror the emotions of others; and compassionate empathy, which moves people to act. But trauma, grief and what’s known as “empathy fatigue” often determine how much empathy people are capable of.
« Lorsque des clients me demandent : “Do: “When clients ask me, ‘Should I be ashamed that I don’t care about his death?’ I see that as a personal judgment piled on top of emotions that are already difficult,” says Ms.<sup></sup> Wandrych. “Often, these questions come from people who pride themselves on being empathetic but feel conflicted when they can’t extend that empathy to someone who hurt them,” the therapist continues.
Elle compare cela à la façon dont les pe: She compares it to how survivors of domestic violence may react to news of their abuser’s death. “If you’ve been abused repeatedly, it’s understandable that you wouldn’t feel sadness when that person is gone,” explains Ms.<sup></sup> Wandrych. “It doesn’t mean you’re cruel, just that you’re human. Our capacity for empathy is shaped by the extent of the harm someone has caused us and by our sense of safety,” she says.
Selon M<sup>me</sup> Wandrych, pour les: According to Ms.<sup></sup> Wandrych, for LGBTQ+ people, these conflicts are amplified by collective trauma. “This year alone, more than 900 bills that could negatively affect transgender and gender-nonconforming people have been introduced,” she points out. “That’s on top of decades of systemic discrimination. When you carry that historical weight, it changes the level of empathy you can – or should – expect of yourself,” she stresses.
Pour M<sup>me</sup> Wandrych, la conclus: For Ms.<sup></sup> Wandrych, the takeaway is that empathy is not unlimited, and that this doesn’t make someone immoral. “These are complex emotions. Almost every feeling people are having right now is valid,” she adds.
Le psychologue Travis Munnerlyn, qui tra: Psychologist Travis Munnerlyn, who works with queer patients in Arizona, shares this view, saying that Charlie Kirk’s assassination creates what is known as “complex trauma.”
« Cette mort n'a aucun sens, nous ne l'a: “This death makes no sense, we didn’t see it coming, and so it’s complicated,” he says. “There are many elements that make this situation complex. So it’s a complex trauma for different people, for different reasons, and the way we grieve someone who has died is personal and individual. It’s ridiculous to think there’s a template we’re all supposed to follow,” he says.
Il précise que, pour les communautés fré: He explains that, for communities frequently targeted by Kirk’s rhetoric, the lack of empathy is less about cruelty than about survival. “It’s not callousness. It’s self-protection,” says Mr. Munnerlyn. “Expecting targeted communities to feel empathy for their aggressors ignores the trauma they’ve lived through. They’ve built narratives to protect themselves, which basically say: ‘This person is dangerous.’ So when the aggressor dies, their reaction may simply be: ‘Good for me.’”
